We need to determine if the graph where each node is an index (or the value) is connected via edges defined by gcd>1 between values.

We have up to 100k numbers, each up to 100k.

We need to check connectivity of the graph where we can move between indices i and j if gcd(nums[i], nums[j])>1. Equivalent to building graph where nodes are numbers (or indices) with edges when they share a prime factor > 1 (i.e., they have any common prime divisor). Indeed, gcd > 1 iff they share at least one prime factor.

Thus, we can think of building a bipartite graph between numbers and their prime factors: each number connects to all its prime factors; two numbers are connected via a path if they share a factor (directly) or through intermediate numbers via common factors.

Thus, connectivity reduces to: all numbers belong to a single connected component in the factor graph.

Approach: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) on indices (or numbers) by unioning numbers that share a prime factor.

Implementation steps:

- If any number equals 1: Since gcd(1, anything)=1, a 1 cannot connect to any other number. So if there is more than one element and any number is 1, answer is false (unless length==1). Actually, if there is a 1 and length>1, impossible to connect to others -> false. If length==1, trivially true (only one element, no pairs). We'll handle that.

- For each number, factorize into its distinct prime factors (we can compute via sieve smallest prime factor up to max(nums) <= 1e5). For each prime factor p, we union the current index with a representative index for that prime factor (maybe store first index that had this prime). We'll maintain a map prime->index (first occurrence). For each number i, for each prime factor p of nums[i]:
   - if p not in map: map[p] = i
   - else: union(i, map[p])

After processing all numbers, we check if all indices belong to same set (i.e., find(0) == find(i) for all i). Alternatively, count unique roots.

Complexities: O(N * log A) for factorization using SPF, plus union-find near O(N α(N)).

Edge Cases: duplicates, numbers with same prime factor.
